title: Endpoint Security Concept Map
subtitle: Attack stages and defensive layers around the endpoint. Tap a bubble.
rootDesc: Protecting every device that connects to the network — laptops, desktops, servers, mobiles, IoT — from being the attacker's initial access point or persistence foothold. Most SOC alerts originate here.

modules.title: Initial Access
modules.desc: The method by which an attacker first gets into the network or onto an endpoint.

children.title: Phishing (T1566)
children.desc: The most common entry path — a malicious attachment or link delivered by email. Mail gateways (e.g. IronPort) sit in front of Exchange to filter these.

children.title: Exploited vulnerability
children.desc: An unpatched CVE in an internet-facing service or client application is abused to gain code execution.

children.title: Valid Accounts (T1078)
children.desc: Logging in with stolen or leaked credentials. Looks like legitimate activity, which is what makes it hard to catch.

modules.title: Execution
modules.desc: Getting code or commands to actually run on the target system.

children.title: PowerShell (T1059.001)
children.desc: A legitimate Windows tool abused for most fileless attacks — no file dropped to disk, so signature-based AV misses it.

children.title: Malicious macro
children.desc: Office document macros that pull down and run the next stage of the payload.

modules.title: Persistence
modules.desc: Techniques that keep the attacker on the system across reboots and logouts.

children.title: Scheduled Task (T1053)
children.desc: The classic route — a task that re-launches the payload on a schedule or at startup.

children.title: Registry Run keys
children.desc: Entries that make Windows launch the payload automatically at each login.

children.title: Service creation
children.desc: Registering the payload as a Windows service so it starts with the system, often with SYSTEM privileges.

modules.title: Privilege Escalation
modules.desc: Moving from a low-privileged account or process up to admin/SYSTEM, usually by abusing a vulnerability or a misconfiguration.

children.title: Kernel / local exploit
children.desc: Abusing an unpatched local vulnerability to jump straight to SYSTEM.

children.title: Misconfiguration abuse
children.desc: Weak service permissions, writable paths, or over-permissive rights handed to a normal user.

modules.title: Defense Evasion
modules.desc: The umbrella set of techniques for avoiding AV/EDR detection.

children.title: Process Injection (T1055)
children.desc: Malicious code is injected into a legitimate system process (explorer.exe, svchost.exe) rather than running standalone — enabling C2 activity without tripping filters.

children.title: LOLBins / Fileless
children.desc: Living-off-the-Land Binaries — abusing built-in, signed Windows tools (PowerShell, WMI, mshta) so nothing malicious is ever written to disk.

children.title: Log clearing
children.desc: Deleting or tampering with event logs to destroy the forensic trail.

modules.title: Credential Access
modules.desc: Stealing passwords and hashes held in memory or on disk — this is what fuels lateral movement.

children.title: LSASS dumping (T1003.001)
children.desc: Reading credentials out of the LSASS process memory. The core purpose of tools like Mimikatz, and critical in a banking environment.

children.title: Credential harvesting from disk
children.desc: Pulling saved passwords from browsers, config files, or scripts left on the host.

modules.title: Lateral Movement
modules.desc: Moving from the first compromised machine to other systems — especially domain controllers and file servers.

children.title: Pass-the-Hash / Ticket
children.desc: Reusing a stolen hash or Kerberos ticket to authenticate elsewhere without knowing the plaintext password.

children.title: Remote services abuse
children.desc: Using RDP, SMB shares, or WMI with valid credentials to reach further into the network.

modules.title: Command and Control
modules.desc: The compromised machine communicating with the attacker's remote server to receive commands and return results — usually disguised to look like legitimate traffic.

children.title: Beaconing
children.desc: Regular, periodic 'check-in' traffic to an unknown domain or IP — the classic signal NDR tools like Darktrace hunt for.

children.title: DNS tunneling
children.desc: Hiding C2 traffic inside DNS queries, which are rarely blocked outright.

children.title: Anomalous process egress
children.desc: A process that should never touch the internet (e.g. notepad.exe) suddenly making outbound connections.

modules.title: Exfiltration
modules.desc: Moving sensitive data out of the target network — via an encrypted channel, DNS tunneling, or cloud storage services.

children.title: Encrypted channel
children.desc: Data sent out over HTTPS or another encrypted protocol so inspection is difficult.

children.title: DLP controls
children.desc: Data Loss Prevention (e.g. Titus) classifies and blocks sensitive data — card numbers, customer records — before it leaves.

modules.title: Impact
modules.desc: The final damage stage of an attack.

children.title: Ransomware
children.desc: Encrypting data for extortion. Around 90% of ransomware incidents start at the endpoint.

children.title: Destruction / DoS
children.desc: Wiping data or systems, or causing service outage.

modules.title: Defensive Controls
modules.desc: The protective layers placed on and around the endpoint.

children.title: AV → EDR → XDR
children.desc: Signature AV catches known files; EDR watches behavior on one endpoint; XDR correlates endpoint with network, email, and cloud.

children.title: Application whitelisting
children.desc: Only approved applications may run (e.g. Solidcore) — everything outside the list is blocked by default.

children.title: Endpoint isolation
children.desc: When a host is judged suspicious, the SOC cuts it off from the network (network containment) while keeping the EDR link alive.

children.title: Patch management
children.desc: Closing known vulnerabilities before they can be exploited — the cheapest control there is.

children.title: Least privilege
children.desc: Users and services get only the rights they need, so a compromise has less room to escalate.
